passages.t: A king taught by a priest
passages.happening:
In the seventh year of Jehu, Joash becomes king and reigns forty years in Jerusalem. His mother is Zibiah of Beersheba (verse 1). ‘And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days he was instructed by Jehoiada the priest’ (verse 2). Yet the high places are not removed, and the people go on sacrificing and burning incense there (verse 3).

Joash tells the priests to collect the money brought into the house of the LORD, the census money, the money from vows and the freewill gifts, and to use it to repair the damage to the temple (verses 4-5). By his twenty-third year, nothing has been repaired (verse 6). He calls Jehoiada and the priests and asks, “Why have you not repaired the damage to the temple?” (verse 7). From now on they are to take no more money for themselves and hand it over for the repairs. The priests agree to stop taking the money and to stop being responsible for the work (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The boy crowned in chapter 11 now grows up and reigns, about 835 to 796 BC, in the years of Jehu and his son in Israel, when Hazael of Damascus dominated the region. The covenant renewal leads naturally to the repair of the LORD's house. Chronicles says Athaliah's sons had broken into it and used its holy things for the Baals. Solomon's temple was by now well over a century old, and its stone, timber and fittings needed work.

The temple had several kinds of income. The census money was the half-shekel ransom paid for each person counted; vow money came from valuations set on people or things dedicated to the LORD; and freewill gifts were voluntary. Each priest seems to have received offerings from the worshipers he served.

The phrase in verse 2, all the days he was instructed by Jehoiada, raises the question of borrowed faith: a life shaped by a mentor's convictions, which may not hold when the mentor is gone.

The account is unusually practical. Its key word is the damage, bedeq, a crack or breach in the building, used again and again. And it contains a quiet criticism. For twenty-three years the priests took the money and did nothing.
passages.later: After the exile Haggai asked a people who had let the LORD's house stand in ruins, “Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” (Haggai 1:4).
passages.asks: The priests collected money for twenty-three years and repaired nothing. Ask what good intentions in your life have never turned into action. And ask whose faith you have been living on, and whether it has become your own.

passages.happening:
Jehoiada takes a chest, bores a hole in its lid and sets it beside the altar, on the right as one enters the house of the LORD. The priests who guard the threshold put into it all the money brought to the temple (verse 9). When the chest is full, the royal scribe and the high priest count the money and tie it in bags (verse 10). They give it to the supervisors of the work, who pay the carpenters, builders, masons and stonecutters, and buy timber and dressed stone (verses 11-12).

The money is not spent on silver basins or trumpets or gold and silver vessels. It goes to the workmen, and with it they repair the house of the LORD (verses 13-14). ‘No accounting was required from the men who received the money to pay the workmen, because they acted with integrity’ (verse 15). The money from guilt offerings and sin offerings stays with the priests (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Coins were not yet used in Judah, so money meant weighed pieces of silver, which is why it was counted and tied in bags. The chest with a hole in its lid took the money out of the priests' hands and made the giving public and accountable. The word for chest, aron, is the same word used for the ark of the covenant, which was itself a box; its holiness came from what it held and what God did there.

Verse 15 is a striking note of trust. The supervisors acted with integrity, emunah, the word for faithfulness that is used of God himself and of the faith by which the righteous live. The guilt and sin offering money stayed with the priests, as the law provided for their support.

The care of the house of worship here is the shared work of king, priests, people and craftsmen. The chapter treats honest handling of money and buildings as part of faithfulness to God.
passages.later: The law set the census money as ‘a ransom for his life when he is counted’ (Exodus 30:12). Paul, carrying a gift for the poor, wrote that he was taking care ‘to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men’ (2 Corinthians 8:21).
passages.asks: The chest made the giving public, and the workmen were trusted because they were honest. Ask what makes you trustworthy with money that is not yours. And ask what structures of accountability help good intentions get carried out where you serve.

passages.t: Treasures for Hazael, and a king killed
passages.happening:
Hazael king of Aram attacks Gath and captures it, and then turns toward Jerusalem (verse 17). Joash takes all the sacred objects dedicated by his fathers Jehoshaphat, Jehoram and Ahaziah, with his own, and all the gold in the treasuries of the LORD's house and the palace, and sends them to Hazael, who withdraws (verse 18).

His servants form a conspiracy and kill him at Beth-millo, on the road down to Silla. Two of them are named, Jozabad son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer. He is buried with his fathers in the City of David, and his son Amaziah reigns (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
Gath, one of the chief Philistine cities, is generally identified with Tell es-Safi, where archaeologists found a siege trench around the city and a destruction layer from the late ninth century BC, which the excavators link to Hazael's campaign. Jerusalem lay only about twenty-five miles to the east, and Joash chose to pay rather than fight.

The chapter contrasts two uses of sacred treasures. In its first half the people's gifts repair the LORD's house. At its end the gifts dedicated by the kings are sent away to buy off an enemy.

The ending is abrupt: conspirators named and no reason given, a pattern that becomes common in the later chapters of Kings. Where Beth-millo and Silla lay is not known with certainty.
passages.later: Chronicles tells of Jehoiada's son, the priest Zechariah, who rebuked the king and his officials: ‘by order of the king, they stoned him in the courtyard of the house of the LORD’ (2 Chronicles 24:21). Jesus spoke of ‘the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary’ (Luke 11:51), and many interpreters identify him with this Zechariah.
passages.hard:
Why does Kings speak so well of Joash, when Chronicles says he turned to idols and had a prophet stoned?

Second Kings says that Joash did right all the days Jehoiada instructed him, and it tells of the temple repair, the payment to Hazael and his murder. Second Chronicles 24 adds that after Jehoiada died, Joash listened to officials who turned to idols, had Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned in the temple court when he rebuked them, and was killed by servants avenging Zechariah's blood.

The two accounts are usually read as filling each other out rather than contradicting each other. The writer of Kings chooses events that fit his concern with worship and the temple, and his careful wording in verse 2 leaves room for a later decline. The Chronicler, writing later for the community after the exile, draws out the moral shape of Joash's life more fully: faithfulness under a mentor, turning away afterward, and judgment. Some scholars think the Chronicler had other sources; others think he interpreted the events theologically. Both works agree on the main shape: a good beginning, a temple restored, pressure from Aram and a violent end.
passages.asks: Joash gave away what had been dedicated to God to buy safety. Ask when it is wise to give up something precious to avoid a greater harm, and when it becomes a failure of trust. And ask what would happen to your faith if the person who taught it to you were gone.
